new_statements.rule_in_words: Denya is described as a register-tone language (H, L, rising, falling, downstepped H); none of the three accessible descriptions makes any statement about word stress, its position, or its absence. No rule for stress placement can be stated from an opened source.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None (no stress statement to have exceptions).
new_statements.domain_note: Mbuagbaw 2002 is a noun-class morphology article by the language's principal describer (CABTAL) with a one-page phonological overview; the tone statement is lexical/word-level (examples are nouns with prefix tones). Bakume 2005 is a comparative D.E.A. thesis whose Denya sketch is of the Takamanda (reference) dialect. Neither is the full phonology (Mbuagbaw 1996/1999), which could not be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: Mbuagbaw 2002 treats Denya as a whole (four dialects: Takamanda, Basho, Betieku, Bajwa; data from a CABTAL language committee). Bakume 2005's phonology sketch is explicitly of the Takamanda reference dialect. Glottolog 5.3 lists deny1238 with alternative names Anyang/Anyah/Nyang/Takamanda/Obonya and no dialect-level glottocodes on the page downloaded. Abangma 1992 calls the language 'Ekoid Bantu'; Mbuagbaw 2002 places it in the Nyang sub-group of Southern Bantoid.

new_statements.quote: 5. TONE Pike (1948) defines as tonal any language ‘having signifant, contrastive , but relative pitch on each syllable.’ Denya is a tone language like most African languages. On the surface Denya has two level tones [ ´ ] and low [ ` ] and two contour tones falling [ ^ ] and rising [ ˇ ]. In addition there is the phenomenon of downstep high being marked /ꜜH/. This will also be discussed below. 5.1 Tonal Phonemes In a tone language, the speaker uses the pitch of his voice to distinguish lexically between morphemes or words that would have been otherwise identical. For example, the following are generally distinguished from each other by tone. /tí/ “to pierce” /tì/ “to wipe” /bé/ “to dance” /bè/ “war” /gèbà/ “area” /gébà/ “bag” /m̀bú/ “dumb” /m̀bù/ “hole”

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the catalog record (tonal, no stress statement): this 1996 phonology is the primary description that Mbuagbaw 2002 p. 66 restates almost word for word (two level tones H/L, falling and rising contours, downstep H) and that Bakume 2005 p. 21 corroborates with the same minimal pairs (tì 'wipe' / tí 'pierce', gèbà / gébà). It adds detail (tone melodies on noun and verb roots, associative-construction tone rules, downdrift/downstep, contour tones as sequences) but nothing on stress, so the catalog cell stands; the bibliography row 'likely states stress; not yet obtained' should become 'read: tonal, silent on stress' with this open the Internet Archive URL.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Denya is described as a tone language: two level tones (H, L), surface falling and rising contours, downstepped H, downdrift; noun roots carry L, H, LH, HL melodies (§5.2), verb roots L, H or LH (§5.4). The monograph has chapters on segments, processes, the syllable and tone but no section on stress or accent, and the words stress/accent/prominence do not occur anywhere in its 96 pages: no word-stress statement.
new_statements.exceptions: none regarding stress; tone: downstep H not found on monosyllabic noun roots (§5.2); semi-vowel offglides never carry their own tone (ch. 4)
new_statements.identity_note: Mbuagbaw's Denya work (per search-engine summaries of the 1996 report) covers the four dialects Takamanda, Basho, Bitieku and Bajwa; Bakume 2005 (held, read earlier) describes the Takamanda dialect.

new_statements.quote: Moreover, Stem 2 (the M-verb root in the F position) has a specific tone pattern depending on whether it is mono- or disyllabic. Abangma writes: The first verb carries low tone, while the second, if monosyllabic, may have either high or low tone depending on the tone of the verb, i.e., it carries the lexical tone. A disyllabic second root morpheme carries a high tone on the first syllable and low tone on the second syllable. The bibliography row 'Seguin 1998.. likely states stress; not yet obtained' can become 'read: tonal in passing, silent on stress' with the t…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule of word stress is given anywhere in the work. Tone is lexical on verb and noun roots (H vs L monosyllabic verbs, L-H disyllabic verbs) and is manipulated by the grammar (subject concord markers change tone with verb mode; plural noun classes 2, 6, 8, 10 take a H-tone associative marker that spreads onto the preceding noun; in class 10 a H replaces the root L). The study is morphosyntactic (Fleming's stratificational model) and defers phonology to Mbuagbaw's 1994 orthography, 1995 tone orthography and 1996 phonology.
